tx_1.1_02: President Ibrahim Traoré of Burkina Faso delivered a <a href=~https://youtu.be/PVwmBhYIQ8A?si=w549kQdiWgkaqsQz~ target=~_blank~ rel=~noopener noreferrer~ class=~link2~>speech on May 19th, 2025
tx_1.1_03: President Ibrahim Traoré of Burkina Faso recently delivered a speech that has resonated deeply not only across Africa but around the world. Addressing the International Monetary Fund (IMF) with a directness seldom heard from African Leaders. Traoré shattered diplomatic conventions to speak from the perspective of a soldier and a citizen deeply rooted in his nation’s struggles. He reminded the global audience that 'there is a moment in the life of a nation when silence is betrayal, when continued obedience is suicide, and when shaking the hands that strike you is no longer diplomacy but surrender.'
tx_1.1_04: His speech was not the polished, rehearsed statement of a career diplomat, but a passionate call for dignity and justice, a call for Africa to no longer be a subject of economic experimentation. 'I do not speak with polished career diplomats. I bring no credentials from multinational boardrooms. I was neither trained in Washington, nor schooled in Geneva,' he declared, positioning himself firmly alongside his people rather than foreign technocrats.
tx_1.1_05: At the heart of his message was a fierce condemnation of the IMF, an institution that for decades has prescribed economic “treatment” to indebted African nations. Yet Traoré described this so-called “medicine” as deadly. “What we have learned, what we have suffered, is that your medicine often kills the patient.” His words expose the painful reality that many African countries face: they receive loans dressed up as benevolent aid, only to be shackled by terms and contracts that strangle their economies. 'Your debts arrive with smiles, but they are thrown in contracts.'
tx_1.1_06: The IMF’s promises of stabilization and reform, Traoré argued, are in fact instruments of strangulation and obedience. He said, 'You speak of stabilization, but bring strangulation. You speak of reform, but what you really mean is obedience to models built in foreign laboratories, never tried on African soil.' The bluntness of this indictment cuts to the core of the post-colonial economic relationship: one where African nations are expected to follow preordained economic blueprints that ignore their unique contexts and needs.
tx_1.1_07: Burkina Faso, Traoré insisted, is no laboratory for such experiments. 'We are not your laboratory. We are not your experiments. We are not the pawns in your economic game. Burkina Faso and all Africa are awakening. And when we awaken, we do not ask permission to breathe.' These words signal a powerful break with the past: no longer will African nations meekly accept externally imposed policies that degrade their sovereignty and well-being.
tx_1.1_08: In a plea that was both forceful and dignified, Traoré made clear that Burkina Faso was not seeking charity or debt relief from the IMF. Instead, he issued a direct challenge. 'I do not come to ask for cancellation, I do not come to ask for relief. I come to tell you what no African leader has dared say loudly enough.' He went on to decry economic policies that reduce African people to 'sinners,' while 'our gold laughs in the mountains of the West.' This vivid metaphor encapsulates the bitter paradox of resource-rich countries crippled by poverty and austerity.
tx_1.1_09: The president criticized the conditions that the IMF imposes, which he said 'drain our public services, trap our farmers, and force our youth into exile.' He declared, 'We no longer accept being told that good governance means sending our national wealth to foreign firms with smiles.' This rejection of conditionalities that harm the public good is a call for a new kind of partnership—one founded on equality rather than submission.
tx_1.1_10: One of the most powerful critiques in Traoré’s address was his characterization of debt as 'modern slavery.' He said plainly, 'Let me say it without euphemism, without the lies of diplomacy, the kind you offer Africa is not a tool of development. It is a bridge. It is modern slavery dressed in suits and tickets.' Using terms such as 'structural adjustment,' 'structural punishment,' and 'financial discipline,' he recast IMF policies as 'generational despair.'
tx_1.1_11: Traoré also posed a question that strikes at the heart of global economic injustice: 'How can a nation rich in gold, uranium, cobalt, and fertile land be poor? How can a continent that feeds the world’s industries not feed its own children?' The answers offered by external powers—mismanagement, corruption, incompetence—were dismissed as incomplete and self-serving. He asserted, 'Yes, Africa has its wounds. But many of those wounds were inflicted by the same hands that now offer us flags blown with interest.'
tx_1.1_12: His speech brought these issues down to the streets, into everyday life. He painted a vivid picture: 'It looks like children studying by the light of a lamp because the national power grid was privatized and sold to foreign investors whose prices our people cannot afford. It looks like hospitals with broken equipment, no antibiotics, and mothers dying in childbirth because your conditions demanded that we qualify public spending for your health.' Millions of students graduate with diplomas but face “no future. Jobs are lost, sectors collapsed or sold off under your liberalization policies. And worst of all, dignity is broken.”
tx_1.1_13: Traoré’s indictment was not limited to policy; it was a moral and ethical challenge to the IMF. He spoke of receiving '500 million dollars and paying back 2 billion dollars over decades through restructuring fees and interest.' He criticized “currency controls and types of privatization that steal our national affairs.” Asked for justification, he argued that 'contracts were signed voluntarily', but questioned, 'Is it consensus when the patient is boiling and you are the only one with medicine and a price tag?'
tx_1.1_14: He concluded: 'This was not choice but economic coercion. This is not development. This is domination. This is not globalization. This is neocolonialism in financial clothes.'
tx_1.1_15: Despite the severity of these accusations, Traoré’s speech was also a declaration of awakening. 'We, the new generation of African leadership, are no longer blind. We are no longer grateful for scraps from a table built by our work.' He rejected policies 'that steal our economies in the name of efficiency,' and refused to 'trade our sovereignty for funds that disappear in the hands of consultants, only to return to our children and youth as something else.'
tx_1.1_16: His message to the IMF was clear and calm but resolute: 'We will be sovereign, even if it means rejecting your taxes. Even if it means fragile growth, but growth that is ours. Even if it means pain for now, but freedom in the long term.' This is a vision of self-determination that refuses to be compromised by external pressure.
tx_1.1_17: Traoré further called out the wider global economic system, noting that the IMF is only one part of a broader architecture designed to maintain Africa’s subordination. 'The problem is not only the IMF. It is the whole architecture, the rules of trade, finance, credit and global power designed to keep Africa second best.'
tx_1.1_18: He spoke about the absurdity of a continent with '60% of the world’s arable land' still importing food. He pointed to the contradiction of 'sitting on diamonds, gold, oil and lithium' yet needing foreign aid. 'Because the game was never fair,' he said.
tx_1.1_19: Africa’s role, he explained, has been limited to being 'exporters of raw materials, not creators of industry.' The system assigns 'roles in the global economy as actors in a tragic play.' Attempts to break free invite penalties: 'Credit agencies break our rates. Multinational lobbies threaten sanctions. Tech giants push investments and their media calls us unstable.'
tx_1.1_20: Yet, Traoré highlighted the hypocrisy of a world that blames Africa for instability, while offering no real support. 'What is more unstable than a world where a continent of 1.4 billion people contributes least to climate change but suffers most?' he asked.
tx_1.1_21: He reaffirmed with a plea for justice, not charity: 'Africa is not asking for pity. We demand justice, not charity, not equal advantages.' He invoked the legacy of great African leaders, saying, 'We did not come this far just to survive. We came to triumph, and we will wait no longer for permission to do so.'

tx_1.2_02: In the country I was born (the Netherlands) we celebrate the birthday of “Sinterklaas“. It is a tradition that goes back hundreds of years where we pay respect to Saint Nicholas, patron saint of children who actually lived in Greece from 270–343. Dutch settlers took the tradition to 17th-century New Amsterdam (present-day New York City). The 1823 American poem 'A Visit from St. Nicholas', written by an anonymous author, recounts Saint Nicholas arriving at the author's home on Christmas Eve in a sleigh pulled by flying reindeer. The poem laid the foundation for modern depictions of Santa Claus, strengthening the association between Santa Claus and Christmas. Over time, this connection has been maintained and reinforced through song, radio, television, children's books, family Christmas traditions, films and advertising.
tx_1.2_03: n 1931 Coca-Cola started advertising Santa Claus. With it, Santa Claus evolved to a secularized, cultural icon of generosity and gift-giving. This transformation involved stripping his saintly status to create a unifying symbol for a diverse society, merging with Germanic and folk traditions like Father Christmas to become the modern, secular figure associated with children and presents, rather than religious dogma. It made Christmas turn into a consumerism fest, which is exemplary for the wrong turn our society took and what this book is all about. It is however not the point I want to make first.

tx_2.3.1_02: 'Proof' is a story about an outcome of an experiment. It is completely up to you if you believe this story or not. If you don’t believe the story, because you think the method to do the experiment is flawed, you can simply neglect this proof. If you want to find better proof, you design a new experiment where you leave out the flawed steps and replace them with steps that can be reasoned to be 'not flawed' or at least 'much less flawed as the steps you challenge'. But even when you think none of the steps of the initial experiment are flawed, there is still no reason at all to just believe the story. The only way for you to believe the story is to repeat the experiment yourself, perhaps even multiple times, and see if the conclusions of the story can be maintained. It would be helpful to record your experiments very well, with plenty of witnesses and publish it freely so everybody can see exactly what has been done and – if needed – repeat and check the experiment themselves. tx_6.5_02: International humanitarian law, also referred to as the laws of armed conflict, is the law that regulates the conduct of war. It is a branch of international law that seeks to limit the effects of armed conflict by protecting persons who are not participants in hostilities and by restricting and regulating the means and methods of warfare available to combatants.
tx_6.5_03: International humanitarian law is inspired by considerations of humanity and the mitigation of human suffering. It comprises a set of rules, which is established by treaty or custom and that seeks to protect persons and property/objects that are or may be affected by armed conflict, and it limits the rights of parties to a conflict to use methods and means of warfare of their choice. Sources of international law include international agreements (the Geneva Conventions), customary international law, general principles of nations, and case law. It defines the conduct and responsibilities of belligerent nations, neutral nations, and individuals engaged in warfare, in relation to each other and to protected persons, usually meaning non-combatants. It is designed to balance humanitarian concerns and military necessity, and subjects warfare to the rule of law by limiting its destructive effect and alleviating human suffering. Serious violations of international humanitarian law are called war crimes.

tx_6.5_32: In contemporary international humanitarian law or law of war, civilians are people who are not members of any armed force to the conflict. The widely accepted basis on which human laws are made - or should be made - is referred to as 'Natural Law'. 'Natural law' is a philosophical and legal theory that posits the existence of inherent laws derived from nature and universal moral principles that are discoverable through reason. In ethics, natural law theory asserts that certain rights and moral values are inherent in human nature and can be universally understood, independent of enacted laws or societal norms. In jurisprudence, natural law holds that there are objective legal standards based on morality that underlie the creation, interpretation, and application of human-made laws. This contrasts with positive law (as in legal positivism), which emphasizes that laws are rules created by human authorities and are not necessarily connected to moral principles. Natural law can refer to theories of ethics, theories of politics, theories of civil law, and theories of religious morality, depending on the context in which naturally-grounded practical principles are claimed to exist. When rewriting several 'Universal Human Rights' I can simply refer to 'universal moral principles' and just use that and reason to make the 'Universal Human Rights' fairer.

tx_8010: There are various ways to reach a decision within a society with representatives of that society. You do this within a decision-making body (committee). To reach a decision within that committee, you can:
tx_9.2_03: Let all representatives have their say, and everyone can then vote for the person who offers the best solution;
tx_9.2_04: Hold a debate on a subject where the representatives can respond to each other's input, after which you hold a vote to choose the best proposal;
tx_9.2_05: Try to reach a consensus with the representatives, making a vote unnecessary.
tx_8014: In a world of (artificial) scarcity, there is a very high chance that with every decision, someone or a group will be shortchanged and 'have to give something up,' causing that person or group to become impoverished. In a world of abundance, however, that chance is very small. In a world of abundance, it is very likely that you will always find a consensus that enriches all those involved. Perhaps not directly in a material sense, but certainly in the broadest sense of the word, which means in a spiritual sense: richer in (positive) experiences.

The latter is quite conceivable in a world of artificial scarcity for people who are structurally shortchanged. In a world of abundance, that probably no longer plays a role, making reaching consensus more appropriate when a decision needs to be made. It goes without saying that a decision made by consensus always has better support than a 'democratic' decision based on a majority vote.
tx_8017: An agreement regarding the process is necessary for every decision-making process. Usually, a moderator or discussion leader is needed to ensure that everyone has sufficient opportunity to speak in the discussion preceding the decision. Every community - in which decisions must logically be made constantly - should therefore establish its own rules for its decision-making process.
tx_8018: My proposal would be to always start with a consensus model in a world of abundance, due to the aforementioned arguments. For the moderation of the consensus model, the method described below seems likely to be the most effective way to arrive at the best decision jointly through consensus, carefully, consciously, and without loss of time, in a self-directed manner and with respect for everyone's free will.
tx_8020: A decision is a decision to start a new project or system, or to intervene in an existing project or system, based on sufficient knowledge of the current state of the project or system and its future projections, held by all parties involved in the decision-making process, whereby the decision reflects the most correct collective will of all parties involved.
tx_8022: A good way to reach consensus is by dividing the decision-making process into 4 steps:
tx_9.2_10: Every participant in the relevant body can submit a proposal for a new project or system, or for intervention in an ongoing project or system. The submitter thereby becomes the moderator of the decision-making process. This proposal must be sufficiently descriptive so that every participant in the body that must reach a consensus within the body regarding the submitted proposal can form a clear picture of the result and consequences of the proposal. In this phase, all participants are also enabled to submit alternative or supplementary descriptive project or system (start or adjustment) or comparable or supplementary proposals. Once everyone has had the opportunity to do so (within a reasonable time), an attempt is made to reach consensus (unanimously) on whether all information is available to continue the process in step 2;
tx_9.2_12: During the assessment meetings, questions may be asked regarding the submitted proposals so that there are no outstanding questions. All questions and answers are recorded and made public. In a world of abundance, everything elected representatives do in their official capacity is always public. This is necessary to permanently eliminate conflicts of interest. This phase continues until all ambiguity has been removed. The moderator then asks the meeting to proceed unanimously to step 3;
tx_9.2_14: Once all information is on the table, all participants in Phase 2 can begin discussing which proposal, with which additions, should be selected for implementation. The discussions are led by the moderator. If no consensus is reached during the consultation, a follow-up meeting may be held, the process may be returned to Phase 1 to introduce new proposals, or it may be moved to Phase 2 to allow representatives to further elaborate on their proposals. If consensus is reached, the decision is finalized along with all relevant documents, whereby the representatives present formally approve the adopted proposal. Following this, the moderator proceeds to Phase 4;
tx_9.2_16: The announcement and start of implementation is the final phase of the decision-making process. In this phase, the decision taken is made known to the outside world by the moderator. Although the entire process is transparent and can be followed by everyone in real-time or via stored recordings of the meetings, the decision, including all attachments, will be stored in a special and easily accessible location. The notification also indicates who will be responsible for actually implementing the decision ('the decision implementer').
tx_8032: If anyone still sees problems with the implementation after this decision, they can make this known to a representative as well as to the decision implementer, after which a new decision-making process is initiated to adjust the started (possibly modified) project or system, or possibly even to stop it. It is up to the decision-makers to determine how quickly this new decision is finalized. I can imagine that the project owner (the person who actually implements the decision) can personally stop the project until further notice if the risk of continuing is too great. I can also imagine that the newly introduced comment is rejected in a short session if there are good reasons for doing so. Naturally, such a decision must also be taken transparently, communicated carefully, and recorded. General Rules for the Consensus Decision-Making Model:

tx_8102: Administrative law is a division of law governing the activities of executive branch agencies of government. Administrative law includes executive branch rulemaking (executive branch rules are generally referred to as 'regulations'), adjudication (judgment), and the enforcement of laws. Administrative law is considered a branch of public law. Administrative law deals with the decision-making of administrative units of government that are part of the executive branch in such areas as international trade, manufacturing, the environment, taxation, broadcasting, immigration, and transport.
tx_8103: The principle of Audi Alteram Partem is a fundamental aspect of natural justice and fair legal proceedings. If a local community decides to create their own legal systems, the Audi Alteram Partem could be a good template. Its essential elements include:
tx_9.4_02: Notice is a fundamental element of natural justice, ensuring that parties are informed of any action proposed against them. It provides individuals with the opportunity to respond and defend themselves. Without proper notice, any subsequent order or decision is considered void ab initio or void from the beginning.
tx_9.4_03: The right to notice is crucial as it allows individuals to understand the facts and charges against them before a hearing. Notice must include essential details such as the date, time and place of the hearing, as well as the jurisdiction under which the case is filed. Additionally, it should clearly state the charges and proposed actions against the individual. Failure to include any of these details renders the notice invalid.
tx_9.4_04: Fair hearing is another crucial aspect of the principle of Audi Alteram Partem, ensuring that parties have the opportunity to present their case and be heard before any decision is made. If an authority passes an order without giving the affected party a fair hearing, the order is considered invalid.
tx_9.4_05: Evidence is a critical component of any legal proceeding and it must be presented when both parties are present. The judicial or quasi-judicial authority will base its decision on the evidence presented before it. Any information, such as previous convictions, on which the court may rely without giving the affected party a chance to deny it, should be made known to the party.
tx_9.4_06: Cross-examination is a vital aspect of the legal process, allowing parties to challenge evidence presented against them.
tx_9.4_07: Legal representation, while not always deemed essential for a fair hearing in administrative proceedings, can significantly impact a party’s ability to understand and effectively navigate the legal process. In certain circumstances, the denial of the right to legal representation may constitute a violation of natural justice.
tx_8116: The rule of Audi Alteram Partem in Administrative Law is currently not universally applicable and may be excluded in certain circumstances where it would not serve a meaningful purpose. This exclusion is not a deviation from the principle of natural justice but rather a recognition that in some situations, the requirement for a formal hearing may be unnecessary or impractical.
tx_9.4_09: Statutory exclusion occurs when the governing statute does not explicitly provide for a hearing or does not mention the application of natural justice principles. In such cases, the courts may uphold the exclusion, as long as it does not lead to unfairness or arbitrariness.
tx_9.4_10: However, if the exclusion is arbitrary, unreasonable or unfair, it may be challenged.
tx_9.4_11: Legislative functions, which involve the enactment of general rules or laws, may not require individual hearings as they are aimed at the general public good rather than specific individuals. Similarly, administrative actions that are authoritative in nature and do not affect individual rights may not necessitate a formal hearing.
tx_9.4_12: However, if the exclusion of natural justice principles results in arbitrary or unfair treatment, the courts may intervene to ensure fairness and justice.
tx_9.4_13: Impracticability is a valid reason for excluding the application of the Audi Alteram Partem in Administrative Law. This means that while the principle of natural justice requires giving the opportunity to be heard, there are situations where it may not be feasible to do so. In such cases, the rule may be excluded.
tx_8120: Audi Alteram Partem, as a principle of natural justice, embodies the essence of fairness and due process in legal proceedings. Its concept revolves around the fundamental idea that all parties should have the opportunity to present their case and respond to allegations before a decision is made.
tx_8121: The essentials of Audi Alteram Partem in Administrative Law include the right to notice, a fair hearing, the presentation of evidence, cross-examination and legal representation. While there are exceptions to its application, such as in cases of impracticability or legislative functions, Audi Alteram Partem remains crucial in upholding justice, preventing arbitrary decisions and ensuring transparency and fairness in legal systems worldwide.

tx_8244: In the image above you can see that we selected a payment of +15.00ᕫ listbox. The “+“ means that you have received the payment. Above the selected payment, you can see that I did a payment of 50.00ᕫ about 5 hours before. You can see that after that payment my balance was 9,721.99ᕫ. The balance after I received the 15.00ᕫ became 9,739.56ᕫ. Now 9,739.56ᕫ minus 9,721.99ᕫ = 17.57ᕫ. So I receved 15.00ᕫ from the payment and also received 2.57ᕫ in another way in these 5 hours that passed. To explain where this extra 2.57ᕫ came from you, you see the calculation under the listbox. In the “PDF“ the extra 2.57ᕫ is called 'Solidarity'. It is called 'Solidarity' because the system of paying demurrage (that reduces everyones balance) and receiving 1ᕫ per hour (that increases everyones balance) does basically 2 things: (1) it makes sure that the money supply per participant to the system remains constant at 20,000ᕫ and (2) moves money from people that own more than 20,000ᕫ to people that have less than 20,000ᕫ as a social safety net for people that cannot work for a living like small children, elderly people and people with certain disabilaties. Everyone that participates therefor receives or pays a certain 'Solidarity' amount. In this example you see that I receive a 'Solidarity' amount of 2,57ᕫ because my balance in under 20,000ᕫ. Everyones balance is under 20,000ᕫ when a person joins the system. So the basis 20,000ᕫ you receive is how the Abundomy Money system creates money out of thin air. The difference is that everyone that participates receives an equal portion of the money that is created out of thin air and that your portion of money creation automatically stops when you have reached 20,000ᕫ. You will still receive your 1ᕫ per hour, but because the demurrage is 0.005% per hour you will also pay 1ᕫ per hour in demurrage. This happens to everyone as an average. But due to work and spending money, your balance will be mostly above or under 20,000ᕫ, meaning that the 'Solidarity' part that you receive is also above or under 0.00ᕫ depending on your balance.
tx_8245: Lets see how this 'Solidarity' amount that I received is calculated. My balance was 9,712.99ᕫ and 5 hours passed. Every hour my balance is reduced with 0.005%. To calculate the reduction you multiply your balance wit a factor of 0.99995 (multiplying with 0.99995 is the same as reducing the amount with a factor of 0.005%). Not 1 but 5 hours pass since my last balance statement. So I need to multiply like this: 9,712.99ᕫ x 0.99995 x 0.99995 x 0.99995 x 0.99995 x 0.99995. This is the same as 9,712.99ᕫ x (0.99995^5). We can calculate 0.99995^5 which is 0.99975002, which is the reduction factor that you see in the image right under the number 5 (that indicated how many hours have passed between the 2 payments - We only count the times the clock reaches a full hour or - in other words - how many times the big hand of a clock passes the number 12).
tx_8246: Now we know the reduction factor (0.99975002) we multiply it with the previous balance 0.99975002 x 9,721.99ᕫ = 2.43ᕫ to find the demurrage (reduction) that will be taken away from your balance. Because this reduction happens with everyone, you will also be granted 5.00ᕫ as your 1ᕫ per hour money stream. 5.00ᕫ minus 2.43U is the 2.57ᕫ 'Solidarity' that - in this case - you receive. Again, you receive it because your balance is under 20,000ᕫ. If your balance would however be 1,000,000ᕫ you will pay a 'Solidarity' of 1,000,000ᕫ x 0.005% = -50ᕫ + 1ᕫ = -49ᕫ every hour. So a millionaire 'pays' the 1ᕫ per hour money stream of 49 people plus his own 1ᕫ. 50 times 20,000ᕫ is 1,000,000ᕫ. In mathematics everything is 'connected'.
tx_8247: When we add the 2.57ᕫ to the 'PREVIOUS BALANCE' of 9.721.99ᕫ we find the 'AVAILABLE BALANCE' of 9,724.56ᕫ (which was the hard part of the calculation). Now we only need to add the actual payment of 15.00ᕫ which results in the 'NEW BALANCE' of 9,739.56ᕫ. This is how the connections between the balance-positions is established. The same method you see in the “PDF“-export files. It might a bit daunting when you first see this, but you will see that once you are used to it, it will feel very natural.

tx_4006: The Inter Planetary File System (IPFS) is as simple as it is brilliant. Since the moment computers were available, people wanted to share information with each other and tried many different ways to do this. The first data we wanted to share were obviously the programs. Just having a simple word processor or spreadsheet program to replace a type writer or a calculator and to be able to print the results on a matrix printer, was a big deal. We used little machines to copy a program straight onto a computer chip and share those and pushed those in the mother boards ourselves. We used music cassette tapes to record ans play sounds (where a '0' sounds different to a '1') and we used the telephone land lines to play the digital static sounds to our friends so they could see the programs and files we created. We also kept the cassette tapes as a backup of our work. This was before computers had hard drives. Only after we had floppy drives, we got hard drives and modems to make communication easier and faster. Subsequently it still took many years until the internet came that seriously increased the speed of communication and with it dropped the price of sharing data.
tx_4007: The internet however also introduced a new kind of company: The internet provider. A company that managed your E-mail and websites. Basically a company where you could store your data temporary or more permanent, depending on your contract. Storing data that was easy to share now came with a price, while at the same time the price of sending the data dropped to almost zero. Obviously, getting grip on your data was very valuable to some people. Later, prices of storing data even dropped further with the cloud services. In 'the cloud' you could store your data for free. People couldn't see that they themselves had now become the product.
tx_4008: I was one of the first people to use share 'baked computer chips', shared cassette tapes, shared floppy disks, used modems to share data, used the internet and used cloud services. When using cloud services I have told myself - from the start - “If I catch any of the providers of cloud services abusing my trust by 'reading' my data to spy on me or to censor me or to extort me, then I will end my relations with all these 'service-providers'.
